statement: Seven-digit numbers are made by arranging all seven of the digits 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3. How many of these numbers are odd?

choices.misconception: I counted all the arrangements and forgot that the number has to be odd.
I only counted the numbers ending in 1 and forgot the ones ending in 3.
I took two thirds of all 210 arrangements because two of the three different digits are odd, but the digits do not appear equally often.
I worked out the numbers ending in 1 and assumed those ending in 3 would give the same count.

hints: An odd number ends in an odd digit. Which digits can go last?
Split by the last digit, 1 or 3. In each case arrange the remaining six digits, remembering that swapping two equal digits does not make a new number.
Ending in 1 leaves 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, with $\frac{6!}{2!\,2!\,2!}$ arrangements. Ending in 3 leaves 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, with $\frac{6!}{3!\,2!}$ arrangements.

solutions.reliable: The last digit must be 1 or 3. If it is 1, the other six digits are 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, which can be arranged in $\frac{720}{2 \times 2 \times 2} = 90$ ways. If it is 3, the others are 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, arranged in $\frac{720}{6 \times 2} = 60$ ways. Total $90 + 60 = 150$. The transferable idea: with repeated objects, divide by the arrangements of each group of equal objects, and split into cases when the cases differ.
solutions.elegant: There are $\frac{7!}{3!\,2!\,2!} = 210$ arrangements, and each of the seven digit cards is equally likely to end up last. Five of the seven cards are odd (three 1s and two 3s), so $\frac{5}{7} \times 210 = 150$ numbers are odd. Weight by cards, not by different digit values.

whyOnTest: Arranging repeated digits tests dividing out equal objects, and the final-digit condition tests whether the cases are weighted correctly.
